I wouldn't have designed PTO (with the advantage of hindsight) had I been the
designers at that time. I don't hate it enough to think it bears removing at
this point but I definitately understand your point of view.

Let me give you an alternative thought on KoR and Rotschek, however. Kiss of
Ra, especially, is a nice answer to the guys who design decks that say, "Shut
up and *NEVER* *ACT*". People who need a million intercept because God
forbid you should ever be allowed to do anything. I realize that "just-go-
into-torpor" is very annoying but certain players really deserve that result.
Besides, it costs 3 blood off of a superior FOR minion so it's not like it's
something that can get pulled very often (like Archon Investigation).

As for Rotschek, I think that falls right into line with other available
combat options and I'm totally confused what your issue is with this. It
would be nicest, of course, if the various combat options worked themselves
out to being more or less a Rock/Paper/Scissors-type game where X tends to
beat Y which tends to beat Z which in turn tends to beat X. But the truth
is, given that one can stick an optional amount of combat into one's deck
and so create an uber-combat-monster deck that beats everything else (almost),
I think it totally makes sense to have something that beats *it* as well.
The real rock/paper/scissors game in combat (IMO) is much more, combat
beating non-combat; more combat beats just plain ol' combat; uber-combat
monster beats more combat; and non-combat beats uber-combat monster because
it just hand-jams it and out-acts to death. (Well, this analysis is VERY
generalized and highly flawed, I realize. But it states my rose-colored-
glasses view of the combat game to the best of my ability.) Having a
Rotschrek-ignore-all-combat-and-send-it-torpor deck fits right in there
somewhere. It's hard to stop and not really that combat-card intensive but
it has definite limitations: only usable once per round and not on one's
own turn. How is this worse than mister Brujah-rush-guy who rushes all
your minions, has enough maneuver to always hit you at close range three
times for total 12 damage, and then Taste of Vitae any blood it loses? Oh,
yea, and plays Immortal Grapple so waxes any fancy non-hand strikes.
Rotschrek is fine in my book.

Fred

Messages.Body:

I'll pick up here to comment on one thought that has recently crossed my
mind regarding PTO, so as to avoid starting an entirely new "ban PTO"
thread.

The thought went something like:
"PTO wallpapers almost every capacity 9/10/11 non-Camarilla vampire with
less than 5 votes."

There's a reasoning behind this thought, which goes something like this:
"Okay, so it's possible to construct inner circle vote decks, which won't
generally have a vampire in play before their 3rd turn, and which can use
PTO.
Now, here's this cool non-Camarilla cap 9/10/11 vampire which I'd like to
build a deck around. He won't come into play until my third turn, either.
How can I defend against an early PTO?
1. Rush the Inner Circle as soon as it shows? This option only even becomes
available if my vampire gets to act before the IC member, and even then, I
have to get past their combat defense (which might be tricky if I'm not cap
11 and they (5 out of 7 IC members, anyway) just Obedience me) an torporize
them (11 cap, but fortunately, only 3 of 7 have for) in a single turn.
Odds: Marginal.
2. Block their action? Unlike PTO (which can target me regardless of seating
because it's not a (D) action), unless I'm in a predator/prey relationship,
this might require a special card (most likely Eagle's Sight) to even be
possible. Even then, must manage a successful block. 5 of 7 IC members have
access to at least one card that will give them 2 extra stealth, so if I
don't have Auspex, my chances of asuccessful block are slim at best. Even if
I do have Aus, 4 of 7 IC members can Elder Impersonate to simply have my
block attempt fail.
Odds: Poor.
3. Delaying Tactics? Sure, and on the next turn? Am I supposed to play an
all DT-deck? Of course maybe I can kill the IC member between turns, but
that would require my deck to be rush combat and even then, there's the
problems as discussed in #1.
Odds: Insignificant.
4. Vote them down? That's 4+1 votes in favor, so unless I have 5 votes (no
vampire so far released does), I can't put the vote down with just my
vampire's voting power. Sure I could toss extra votes, and 4 of 7 IC members
have superior Presence. I'll always need the rest of the table on my side to
even have a chance.
Odds: Insiginificant.
5. Play Camarilla. Sorry, I said non-Camarilla vampire.
Odds: Nil.
...
Oh great, I can't."

Granted, there are other cards (like Kiss of Ra or Rötschreck) that can be
best defended against by playing a particular type/style of deck (e.g. using
for or intercept wall, respectively), but none of them are anywhere near as
effective as PTO (e.g. Kiss of Ra is more expensive and less devastating;
Rötschreck is harder to play and less devastating).

Obvioulsy, one could argue that PTO has a fairly high opportunity cost, but
honestly, "have a non-camarilla vampire worth targetting" doesn't sound that
bad to me, with two or more non-Camarilla decks at a five player table being
an odds-on bet by number of vampires ever printed.

Then again, one could argue that
EQ 1. Arika + Protect Thine Own = Freakin' totally Broken!
After all, Arika has all four disciplines useful in obliterating defense
strategies (see discussion above) at superior. The odds of a 10 cap
non-Camarilla vampire stopping Arika from PTOing him are, first
aprroximation, nil.

That as and of itself seems like conclusive proof that, at the very least,
one of the two cards named in EQ. 1 must be modified, because this is VTES
and not the M-game, and we don't want "unstoppable" combos. Or so I hope.

Thomas Pichler

On 23 Feb 2005 01:01:43 -0800, "Joscha" <joscha...@gmx.de> wrote:

>I'm in favour of banning DU/KR as I now understood, what the reasons
>were. I like the change of Anarch Revolt, as I was annoyed by decks
>which were relying heavy on it. These three cards were spoiling
>regularly whole rounds.

Yesterday we played two games using the new wording of Anarch Revolt.

It was included in a vote deck with some Banishment to boost. At the
first table it was generally useless until the endgame since everyone
were able to quickly turn someone into anarchy. But it had a great
deal of effectiveness when both the vote deck and a cross-table player
got 1 VP each, one immediatelly after another.
I was the unlucky one to be the vote deck's predator, got a clogged
hand full of combat I couldn't use (bruise n' bleed, eh?) and my War
Ghoul predator was ousted after torporizing half of my minions and
reduce me to 3 pool.
Facing two opponents with few pool, at least one less vampire lost on
combat, with 3 Anarch Revolts on the table and saving the Banishments
for the right moment, the vote deck's player had no trouble banishing
the anarchs me and his prey controlled. He almost ousted the two in
the same turn.

At the second table, it had a very similar effect, but with the caveat
that both me and my new prey (this time I got 1 VP) completely forgot
to become anarch and we payed a very high price for it: the vote
deck's player had 2 master phase actions and played two more AR's. I
had 6 pool at the time, was about to Corrupt another minion (just 1
more counter needed), but a KRC punished me for being too harsh on
stealing minions and not protecting my pool :-/ The vote player faced
a new prey with around 15 pool and could not prevent him from becoming
anarch, but his early 3 damage certainly helped along that path.

General conclusion I've personally taken: careful planning and play
still renders Anarch Revolt very useful and even powerful on a vote
deck without harming everyone around, exactly like it was predicted.
In fact, it seems less sketchy to pull out the AR/Banishment combo
than I initially thought. Almost everyone used a low- or midcap
vampire that could become anarch, and almost no one took some
preventive measure like turning *two* vampires anarch since they
needed the available actions to do something (perceived) better, even
after seeing Banishment.

<IANALSJ>

(And I'm not necessarily talking directly about what LSJ said, more
about why anti-vote is hard.)

When you get bled, you can attempt to block the same as against a
political action. However, a political action starts at +1 stealth.
Also however, a political action is blockable by two different people
not just one, so this sort of evens out. So this isn't really an area
for concern, IMO. You may need stealth on either.

Once you get into the referendum, pro-vote cards tend to be
significantly stronger than anti-vote (i.e. gain votes and vote it down)
cards - the hot anti-vote cards are stuck in Presence, largely. It's
unlikely that you'll play "all your action modifiers" - in many
instances, a superior Bewitching Oration will do a lot, so you don't
need to play the Awe in your hand, or whatever else you might be
holding. (Telepathic Vote Counting, say.) So many times, the vote will
be passing with relatively few cards played. If it's tight the other
way, a big cap will often do well with Awe. Bear in mind that every
blood Awe costs you could be sucked back up by a Voter Captivation -
something you don't get on bleed actions! ("Oh yeah, I'll just burn
these three or four blood to get some extra bleed, and suck it back up
when done.") And Voter Captivation is a strong card which can turn all
damage votes into pool gain votes - and pool gain votes into super pool
gain votes!

Once you start applying the action of the vote, you can get (say) 5
unbounceable pool theft (Parity Shift) or 3 pool damage (KRC) - unlike a
bleed, where you could reduce the bleed, bounce the bleed or so on.
Referendum modifiers give you the potential for that - unbounceable,
unreduceable (ugh) pool loss. This isn't something that bleed can ever
give you by itself. And, as others have expounded about stealth-bleed,
repetitive actions for 3 bleed can be strong (even if 5 or 6 might be
even better), so a well-played vote deck can still do a LOT of damage.

Additionally, many decks will bleed incidentally (unless they have
Protected Race-horses, which is a significantly double-edged card, even
if potentially very good), whereas 90% of votes come much less
frequently - they need to be in the deck, for a start. This means that
pro-vote tech (Awe, BO etc.) is much less likely to find resistance and
anti-vote tech is much riskier. Thus, when you do have anti-vote tech,
it needs to be quite strong or you just don't put it in. Whereas you
can happily put in Telepathic Counter (say) and not worry too much about
it not being as great as some other bleed defence card, it can still be
good enough and ranks high on the "likely to be a valid, useful play"
scale.

What I would like to see are more pieces of vote defence tech which are
"good enough" but in different ways so that DT is not a no-brainer and
other tactics may be stronger or more useful for different decks, but
which don't unnecessarily hamper the vote deck either.

</IANALSJ>

Ages back, various people were talking about bounce and why it's so
great - and I agree, bleed bounce is great. But it's possible to
formulate other cards that are strong, without being bounce.

I think I once suggested something like a reaction where the acting
vampire took one damage for each bleed they inflicted. Not that that
would be a good card to print, of course, but you can see the point -
it's possible to have a good card that works very differently to bounce
whilst not necessarily detracting from bounce.

Having been a counterspell player for about 10 years, allow me to
explain why I do not think DI is good:

PROS OF COUNTERSPELL
1.) Counterspell is cheaper than what your opponent does. Counterspell
costs 2 mana. Unless they have a DANGEROUS spell which costs 1, your
Counterspell will not cost more--and even if they have something which
costs 1, it's still pretty good, because they will often not cast
another spell before you untap.

[DI will usually cost you MORE that your opponent's card, since it
costs 1 MPA and is only usable on things which cost 0 MPA. Your
opponent will probably do something else before you can play another
one.]

2.) Playing a Counterspell requires only that your opponent play any
spell which has the potential to kill you or your stuff--any creature,
any removal spell, almost anything. In a tournament deck, most cards
your opponent plays will be able to do damage or control the board in
SOME capacity. Therefore, Counterspell will (almost) always be
playable, and is always 1-for-1.

[As Fred points out, Jyhad players often send multiple small threats,
none of which are the heart of the problem, and none of which are
obviously the thing to play DI on. Take Scouting-Lost-Cloak-Threats
for example: Is DI any good against such piecemeal offense? And
because we replace cards, "card economy" and "1-for-1" mean different
things in Jyhad than in M:TG.]

LIMITATIONS OF COUNTERSPELL
Counterspell can't counter lands that will kill you (Mishra's Factory,
etc.)

I do think non-spells (in M:TG) and non-minion cards (in V:TES) are
comparable here.

However, although DI has the same (few) limitations as Counterspell, it
does not have all of the pros--mainly, the fact that it usually costs
more (because of the MPA). Additionally, having Counterspell in one's
hand doesn't prevent one from having another card as well. (Blue likes
to draw cards, so they can have Counterspell and other things.) But in
V:TES, DI counts against your hand. Every DI you have means another
card you can't have--how come a hand with 3 Counterspells is great,
while a hand with 3 DI's is crap?

And don't forget that if M:TG players always drew up to 7 cards,
Counterspell decks would probably not exist at all.

I think I should add that in 2-player games, attrition is great,
whereas in 5 player games, attrition is less so.

Lastly, perhaps most importantly, you can't DI everything. You CAN
Counterspell everything.

-- Brian
North American Continental Champion 2003
I never play DI.

In VTES there are only a few truly significant events--inflection

biggest one is the seat switch which has thankfully gone away (and some

significantly affect these crucial inflection points in ways that no

the choice of a deck archetype is 'above, outside, over' the rules

game. Thus, the craft of making this choice to gain advantage is
called 'the metagame'. But by the same token, it has no meaning to,
for instance, call one deck a "metadeck" because its success or
failure operates by different rules than most decks. (I suppose
Anarch Revolt would be an example of that.)

vs. the effect you want to get from it to make it worthwhile.
Nothing in all of this suggests the term "above" to me. Just
different. It still has a cost; that cost still needs to be
taken into account.

A better example than this that I can think of is actually
Storage Annex. That card has just about ZERO downside that I
can find. (You can only access the card every master phase
and it can be lost through burning or losing the SA - but these
are really hardly anything.) Yet, it's not a god card, even
so. It's a likable card, to be sure. But even for decks that
need the storage, it can hard to squeeze in. Its upside has
trouble getting above its opportunity cost (Blood Dolls and
such).

Actually, not necessarily - especially in a multiplayer game. Of course,
it always depends on the players, their personalities and objectives, their
decks, the metagame interaction between their decks, and luck. But quite
often in a game, an event will tend to be equilibrated over time as players
gang up on the leader and cross-table cooperation props up a weak player
who's allies feel is required to hold down his predator and prey. Ergo,
often quite the opposite turns out to be true: something early and
significant tends to get lost in subsequent play, like a boat's wake getting
lost in random waves.

Fred

Many things have been said already, I won't address them directly, just
add my opinion for what it's worth, and maybe point out some things that
haven't been addressed in exactly this way, or just put together some of
the most pertinent things (IMO) already said :

- I do not believe that 1 pool and a MPA are HIGH opportunity cost : a
DI can "kill" a PTO / Banishment (cards with enormous effects but that
few decks are full of) better than a Delaying Tactics ; it can kill a
Deflection on your face, a War Ghoul (always good to gain time), a
Conditionning, a rush, an IG... Many cards which have a huge impact on
your game. 1 pool and a MPA aren't "high cost" for any of these things,
let alone the wide choice of uses.

- There are cards that are good in a deck even if you put 1 or 2 of
them. How many Kine Dominance or Far Mastery will one include in a deck
? But it's the difference between losing your Hunting Ground / War Ghoul
/ Whatever or not.

- Many good decks are a little toolboxy (the Eurobrujah being a
tournament winning example : it may include fight, bleed, reactions,
maybe votes...). It will be slowed down a lot if it looses an Anathema,
a Govern, a Deflect, an IG, a Graverobbing, etc.

- Some decks will rely heavily on a few copies of an important object,
say, the Eye of Hazimel. DI will delay the working of such a deck
considerably.

- Sure, playing DI requires some skill, as did the change of places ;
but this is a game of skill, isn't it, and good cards are really good in
the hands of good players ; a bad player will make mistakes on rushes,
bleeds, reactions, as well as DI. So I won't go any further in that
useless angle of the discussion.

- To succeed in an action at Jyhad isn't playing one card, but several :
the action, probably some stealth and other modifiers ; a good player
will find the weakest element and DI it. For instance, the player has
been stuck on stealth for a while, and has patiently waited to get what
he needed. He thought it all, now it could work, he does it... DI !!
Start all over again. This happens all the time.

- Yes, DI is the most efficient on cards playable only once. This
includes : reaction cards playable by the same minion (redirections of
all kinds from your predator...), the dreaded Immortal Grapple (and one
less may be one more minion for you), Conditionning (yes, I've lost or
won more than a few games because of a DIed bleed modifier at the right
timing), and of course Ancient Influence, Reins of Power... It's a lot
already, and doesn't mean it's not useful on other cards !!

- there are some ways to get the DI when you most need it and not keep
it in hand ; the more frustrating use I saw is with the Ercyies
fragment, when my prey took it from my grand' prey's ash heap at the
very moment she needed it, and countered my killing bleed by cancelling
one of the cards of my combo (I didn't have the chance to get it back
and Time Limit took its toll).

- I had a luck to make it this year to the finals of the biggest french
tournament, where I was the only one to die, LOL. One of the best
players in the country, and incidently among the best 10 in the world,
told me "it's normal, you didn't pack enough defenses : most of the
players on this final table have 6 DI and 6 DT, that's what's needed at
this level in the current metagame" (please Kamel feel free to correct
me it these aren't your exact words). As of me, I had the place for only
2 DI in the deck, and please believe I always found use for them.

All these elements have concurred over the years to make me hate DI : it
does way too many crucial things, and its very existence affects the
game in a bad way. It exists, I'd rather not, but as it does I must take
it into account with every card I play, which isn't normal IMO, and
certainly makes it a very, very overpowered card.

Yours Deadly,

Orpheus

3 [metaphysics] : more comprehensive : transcending <metapsychology> --

It's there. I posted this particular sub-definition because it seems

I don't think there is a such thing as a "meta-card", as no card can be
'a card in a different way from standard cards, but designed to deal
with them'. Unless V:TES does something like Sensei cards in L5R,
which was a horrible idea, which they did away with.

Direct Intervention isn't above or beyond, in fact I'd say it goes
right for what it does--no frills, no fanciness, very direct. More
than any other card, it gets right to the point. "Direct" is this
card's first name. :)

DI isn't above or beyond, because cancelling another card is a big part
of the game--Undead Strength vs. Skin of Rock, Enhanced Senses vs. Lost
in Crowds, Threats vs. Telepathic Misdirection, Maneuver vs. Maneuver,
etc. DI has them all covered, without any requirements--and also costs
way more. If there was a combat card that gave a vampire a maneuver, a
press, +1 strength, prevent 2 damage, or an additional strike, but cost
a MPA, I would likewise think it was no "meta-card", and also
versatile, and also overcosted.

DI has never been a big part of my game. I don't play it, and when it
gets played on me, it never affects me in a huge way, since pretty much
if you cancel my card, I'll play another. Works for combat cards,
actions, even +intercept and -stealth cards, since they're mostly
interchangeable. Other than bounce, I probably don't care.

-- Brian
